strengths: The method is validated at real scale on both a dense (Qwen3-1.7B) and a large MoE (Qwen3-30B-A3B) model, which goes beyond the ~1B-scale experiments of the closest prior work (MOR) and demonstrates practical applicability.
Consistent positive gains across 17 diverse benchmarks (avg +0.87 on 30B MoE, +1.88 on 1.7B dense) with a very small parameter increase (~0.03M routers).

Reasonably thorough ablations: router controlling loss vs. threshold control vs. z-loss baseline, selection ratio (10/20/30%), and layer placement (Ls:Le), plus training-dynamics visualizations (Figs. 4-5) that directly support the design choices.
A clear formal FLOPs overhead analysis in the appendix (~6.27%) rather than vague efficiency claims, and honest positioning against MOR in a dedicated comparison table.
Interesting qualitative analyses (layer-wise token selection patterns) that provide interpretability beyond raw accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to closely related work (Mixture-of-Depths, MOR, ITT). The core idea — token-choice routing for selective reprocessing with re-weighted output fusion — is a straightforward combination; the main new contributions are engineering-level loss functions (entropy dispersion + MSE centering) and a threshold controller, which feel incremental.

No compute-matched baseline. DND adds ~6.3% FLOPs, but the comparison is against a vanilla SFT model of equal size. There is no control showing that simply training the vanilla model for the equivalent extra compute (or a slightly deeper/wider model, or standard depth-recurrence on all tokens) would not achieve similar gains; the reported +0.87% average gain for +6% compute is modest and the efficiency claim is thus weakly supported.

No direct empirical comparison with the closest baselines (MOR, ITT, MoD). The paper only argues differences in a table rather than benchmarking them under comparable settings, making it hard to judge the marginal value of the proposed control schemes.

Some reported SFT baseline numbers are surprising (e.g., AIME24 jumping from 28.33 to 51.46, MMLU from 80.12 to 85.41 after SFT), and the training data (1-2M synthetic instances) is described only vaguely. The confound between the SFT recipe and the DND gains is not fully disentangled, and no variance/statistical significance is reported despite gains often under 1 point.

Inconsistencies and clarity issues: PIQA is listed as a benchmark but absent from Table 1; the appendix renames DND to 'Drop-and-Drop'; positional-embedding handling in the Pack/Unpack operator (E'_pos) for RoPE-based models is not explained, which matters for reproducibility.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or data release is mentioned, hyperparameter sensitivity (λsd, λdp, α, γ, buffer sizes) is only coarsely ablated, and several design choices (sigmoid vs. softmax routing, β fusion) lack justification against simpler alternatives.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: adaptive token-level computation for LLMs, combining token selection with latent-depth test-time scaling.
The method is applied at genuine scale (Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE in addition to a 1.7B dense model), which is more convincing than many adaptive-computation papers that stop at small models.

Comprehensive benchmark suite (17 benchmarks across knowledge, math, coding, and agent tasks) and a reasonably detailed ablation study over the routing losses, threshold control, selection ratio, and layer placement.
The analysis of threshold dynamics and selection ratio stability during training (Figs. 4-5) and the qualitative token-selection visualizations provide some insight into the mechanism.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core idea is a straightforward combination of token-choice routing (as in MoE) with layer re-processing, closely building on Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024), Mixture-of-Recursions (Bae et al., 2025), and ITT (Chen et al., 2025). The delta is mostly an engineering-oriented training strategy (entropy dispersion loss + MSE preservation loss + a threshold PI controller with EMA) that is ad hoc and lacks theoretical motivation.

Weak baselines. The only comparison is the same model SFT'd without DND. There are no comparisons against the closely related methods (MOR, ITT) even in a re-implemented form, nor against simpler compute-matched alternatives such as SFT for longer, uniformly adding depth, or a fixed top-k selection without the proposed control machinery. As a result, the claimed advantage of the 'precise ratio control' over z-loss-style alternatives is supported only by internal ablation, not by external baselines.

Small gains without significance analysis. The headline +0.87 average on the 30B model and +1.88 on the 1.7B are modest; no variance, standard errors, or repeated runs are reported (even AIME24 with 16 samples per question is averaged without uncertainty). Some per-benchmark deltas (e.g., +0.13 BBH, +0.15 MATH) are likely within run-to-run noise.

Ambiguous methodological details. It is unclear how attention operates in the nested pass: selected tokens are packed into a compact sequence with new positional embeddings E'_pos, but whether they attend only to each other (losing context from unselected tokens) or to the full sequence (which would complicate the FLOPs analysis and the no-information-leakage argument) is never specified. How the training loss treats selected vs. unselected tokens in the fused output is also unstated.

No actual inference-cost measurements. The paper claims 'minimal computing increase' but only provides a theoretical FLOPs analysis in the appendix; wall-clock latency, throughput, and memory are absent despite the pack/unpack scatter operations and variable-length nested passes being potentially expensive in practice.

Attribution of gains is questionable. Because the DND model receives additional SFT with extra trainable parameters and extra forward computation, part of the improvement may simply come from more effective training compute rather than the routing mechanism; a compute- and data-matched control is not provided. Moreover, the ablation shows that even without the proposed training strategies (the paper's central contribution) the DND architecture alone yields 1.01-1.15 of the 1.88 gain, weakening the claimed importance of the control scheme.
Reproducibility concerns: the training data is described only as 'synthetic material built upon a seed set of 1-2 million instances' with no details or release; no code release is mentioned.

Carelessness that undermines confidence: the appendix renames the method 'Drop-and-Drop (DND)' inconsistent with the title; Table 1 contains a typo ('wothout'); the appendix states the initial/final four layers are excluded from a 48-layer model yet sets Le = 43; PIQA is listed in the benchmark section but missing from Table 1; Fig. 3(c) references equations in a confusing way.

Claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'precise and stable control over any predefined selection ratio target' and 'without any performance degradation' are asserted from a single configuration on two models.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the method (token-choice routing + nested re-processing + normalized fusion) is described in sufficient detail to follow and potentially reproduce, including all key hyperparameters in the appendix.

Evaluation is broad: 17 benchmarks spanning general knowledge, math/STEM, and coding/agent tasks, on both a dense model (Qwen3-1.7B) and a large MoE model (Qwen3-30B-A3B), showing consistent (if modest) improvements with no regressions.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: the contribution of the router controlling loss and threshold control scheme is isolated against a simpler z-loss-like variant (1.88 vs 1.01 average gain on Qwen3-1.7B), and key architectural hyperparameters (selection ratio, layer range) are explored.

The training-dynamics analyses (Figs. 4-5) concretely demonstrate that the proposed buffer proportional control and EMA synchronization stabilize the selection ratio, directly supporting the claimed design choices.
The method is parameter-efficient (0.03M extra parameters) and the FLOPs overhead analysis (~6.3% for the 30B model) is a useful transparency addition.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea (dynamically routing a subset of tokens through an additional transformer layer pass) is a straightforward combination of Mixture-of-Depths token-choice routing (Raposo et al., 2024) and recurrent-depth/latent-reasoning ideas (MOR, ITT, looped transformers). The training strategies (entropy-based dispersion loss, MSE preservation loss, threshold EMA) are sensible engineering but incremental.

No empirical comparison against the closest prior methods. The paper claims superiority over MOR's z-loss-based selection but only compares against its own ablated variant; there is no head-to-head evaluation with MOR, ITT, or a uniform-extra-depth baseline (i.e., reprocessing all tokens or a fixed random subset), which is essential to show the dynamic selection itself — rather than simply extra computation plus additional SFT — drives the gains.

Gains are small: +0.87 average on the 30B MoE model and +1.88 on the 1.7B model, with no statistical significance testing, variance over seeds, or error bars (especially problematic for noisy benchmarks like AIME24 with 16-sample averaging).

Potential confound: the DND model and baseline both undergo SFT, but the SFT data is only described as '1-2 million instances with significant synthetic material'; it is not fully clear the comparison is data-matched, and only two models from a single model family (Qwen3) are tested, limiting generalizability claims.

Efficiency claims are under-supported: the overhead is analyzed only analytically in FLOPs; no wall-clock latency or throughput measurements are reported, despite dynamic selection typically incurring kernel/packing overheads that dominate realized speed.
The fusion mechanism introduces a learnable scalar β modulated by p^i, but no ablation of the fusion strategy itself is provided, and the behavior of β after training is not analyzed.
No code release or artifacts are mentioned, which weakens reproducibility for a systems-oriented contribution.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation across four models (three dense 1B-scale models and a 30B MoE), covering a broad suite of 17+ benchmarks spanning knowledge, math, reasoning, and coding domains
Consistent, non-degrading gains across all models and most benchmarks (+1.88 to +2.61 average on dense models, +0.87 on the 30B MoE), which is meaningful for a plug-and-play post-training method
Thorough ablation study (router controlling loss, threshold control, selection ratio, layer ranges) that isolates the contribution of each proposed component

Thoughtful mechanism analyses: correlation between token selection and logit entropy, layer-wise selection patterns, threshold dynamics visualization, and qualitative token-level visualizations supporting the 'critical token' hypothesis

Practical systems evaluation: FLOPs overhead analysis (~6.27%), end-to-end throughput measurements with vLLM/SGLang on real hardware (91.6–93.1% of vanilla speed), and honest reporting of the speed cost
Clear positioning against the closest related works (MOR, ITT, Mixture-of-Depths) with a detailed comparison table in the appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea—routing a subset of tokens through extra transformer depth—is very close to existing work (ITT, MOR, Mixture-of-Depths). The contribution is primarily the post-training adaptation plus routing/threshold control engineering (entropy-based dispersion loss, MSE preservation loss, EMA threshold control), which feels incremental

Missing the most important control baseline: a vanilla SFT run with matched additional training compute (e.g., ~6-8% more steps or data). Since DND adds computation during training too, part of the gain may come simply from extra effective training rather than dynamic nested depth. The ITT comparison partially addresses this but is only reported for one model with a tiny margin (+0.05 over baseline SFT)
No statistical significance testing or seed/variance reporting. Several gains on the 30B MoE model are small and plausibly within noise (e.g., +0.13 BBH, +0.15 MATH), making the +0.87 average fragile

The framing as an 'efficiency' contribution is questionable: DND increases both training and inference compute (~6-8% FLOPs, 7-9% throughput loss) to buy ~1-2 accuracy points. The proper comparison is against spending that same extra compute uniformly, and the accuracy-per-FLOP trade-off versus simply deepening the model or extending SFT is not analyzed

Some technical details are under-specified or confusing: the treatment of positional embeddings for the packed nested sequence (E'pos), whether selected tokens attend to each other during the nested pass (which could distort causal structure), and Appendix A even mislabels the method as 'Drop-and-Drop'

The claimed 'natural next step' from binary pruning to selective re-processing is a plausible but not strongly justified design; there is no comparison against simpler alternatives such as uniform (non-adaptive) re-processing of a fixed 20% of tokens, which would directly test whether the dynamic routing is actually necessary

Reported layer-range ablation results (5:22 and 3:24 variants outperforming on some benchmarks but lower overall) and the choice to fix configuration from 1.7B ablations for the 30B model leave open questions about transferability of hyperparameters

strengths: The method is applied end-to-end to multiple real models, including a 30B-scale MoE model (Qwen3-30B-A3B), which is more convincing than many adaptive-compute papers that only test small models.
Evaluation spans a broad suite of benchmarks (knowledge, math, coding, agentic), and the paper reports practical throughput measurements with vLLM rather than only theoretical FLOPs.
There is a reasonably detailed ablation of the training strategies (router controlling loss, threshold control/EMA), selection ratio, and layer range, plus qualitative token-selection visualizations.
The post-training, plug-and-play framing is practical: it avoids the enormous pretraining cost required by related approaches like MOR.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea—dynamically routing a subset of tokens through an extra pass of the same layer—is essentially a token-choice variant of Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024) and is very close to ITT (Chen et al., 2025) and MOR (Bae et al., 2025). The paper's own ablation (Tab. 4) shows the truly 'novel' components (router controlling loss, threshold control) contribute only ~0.8 of the 1.88 average gain; the bulk comes from the Bearer [REDACTED] mechanism already present in prior work.

Weak cost-benefit justification: the method costs ~6% extra FLOPs and 7-9% throughput loss to obtain +0.87 average points on the 30B model (and ~1-2.6 points on 1B models). The paper does not compare against simpler compute-matched alternatives, e.g., uniformly applying an extra layer/pass during SFT, longer SFT on the baseline, or other latent test-time scaling baselines beyond ITT.

The claimed superiority over ITT (attributed to top-P selection mismatch and information leakage) is asserted but not experimentally isolated; ITT is compared only at the aggregate result level, without an ablation swapping in token-choice routing for ITT to support the causal explanation.

No statistical significance or variance reporting: gains such as +0.87 average on 17 benchmarks, with individual deltas as small as +0.13 (BBH) and +0.15 (MATH), are within plausible run-to-run noise given no seed variation or confidence intervals.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: Appendix B states Ls=4, Le=43 for the 48-layer model but the ablation table and text reference layer ranges like 4:23; Sec. 4.5/Fig. 5 attribute ratio stabilization to EMA while Fig. 5a/5b and Fig. 6 captions conflate buffer proportional control and EMA synchronization; typos such as 'wothout' in Table 2.

The two proposed losses are only heuristically motivated and partially contradictory (entropy-based dispersion pushes scores apart while MSE pulls all scores toward 0.5); there is no theoretical or empirical analysis of what joint distribution they induce, and no analysis of failure modes.

Reproducibility concerns: the training data (1-2M instances of 'synthetic material') is described only vaguely, no dataset composition or decontamination details are given, and code is only promised. This is especially important because SFT gains may be partly attributable to the extra data/epochs rather than the architecture.

The analysis in Sec. 4.5 is correlational and post-hoc: higher logit entropy correlating with selection (Pearson r = 0.34) is weak evidence, and the entropy decrease after DND could be a trivial consequence of additional computation rather than evidence of better representations.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the method (token-choice routing + nested re-processing + normalized fusion + threshold control) is described in enough detail to understand and largely reimplement, including hyperparameters in the appendix.

Evaluation breadth is a strength: three dense models plus a 30B MoE, a large benchmark suite spanning knowledge, math, coding, and agent tasks, and practical throughput measurements on vLLM/H100 rather than only FLOPs accounting.

The ablation study (Table 4) is reasonably thorough, covering the router controlling loss, threshold control, selection ratio, and layer ranges, and the training-dynamics visualizations (Figs. 5-6) provide direct evidence that the proposed stabilizers work as intended.

The analysis of which tokens get selected (entropy correlation, Fig. 4a/4b, layer-wise selection patterns) is an interesting empirical contribution that supports the core motivation, even if the correlation strength is modest.

The post-training 'plug-and-play' positioning is practically valuable compared to MOR, which requires training from scratch on 200B+ tokens; the distinction with prior work is articulated clearly (Table 6).
weaknesses: Limited novelty over closely related work. The core idea — routing a subset of tokens through extra recurrent depth — is a direct combination of Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024), ITT (Chen et al., 2025), and MOR (Bae et al., 2025) applied in a post-training setting. The main genuinely new elements (score dispersion/distribution-preservation losses, buffer proportional control, EMA threshold synchronization) are incremental engineering heuristics rather than conceptual advances.

The critical compute-matched baseline is missing. DND adds ~6% FLOPs during training and inference (Table 3 shows a 7-9% throughput penalty). The proper comparison is plain SFT with the same additional compute budget (e.g., longer training, deeper layers, or more data). Without it, it is impossible to attribute the +0.87-2.6 point gains to the DND mechanism rather than to the extra training/inference compute.

Gains at scale are marginal and possibly within noise. The 30B MoE result (+0.87 average, with BBH at +0.13, MATH at +0.15) comes with no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests; many per-task deltas are small enough to plausibly be run-to-run variance, especially given the reported AIME24 protocol of 16 samples.

Baseline comparison to ITT is thin: it appears only in the Qwen3-1.7B row of Table 1 (+0.05 over baseline), and is not evaluated on Llama/Gemma or the 30B model. A stronger and more complete head-to-head against the most related method is needed to substantiate the central claim that the proposed routing control is what matters.

Inconsistencies between the benchmark list and the reported tables: Sec. 4.1 lists DROP, CMMLU, MATH-500, AIME24, MBPP+ etc., but Table 1 (dense models) reports only 12 benchmarks and omits several; it is unclear whether some benchmarks were selectively reported.

Some presentation issues undermine confidence: the appendix refers to 'Drop-and-Drop (DND) policy' while the text defines DND as 'Dynamic Nested Depth'; Fig. 4a reports Pearson r = 0.336, which is a weak correlation presented as validation; Table 2's reference models (Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-30B-A3B Chat) are under-different non-baselines.

Reproducibility concerns: code is only 'to be released', and the SFT data (a 'significant volume of synthetic material' on a 1-2M seed set) is described too vaguely to reproduce — this is particularly problematic because the SFT mixture could itself drive part of the improvement.

The threshold control scheme (proportional gain + EMA toward top-k quantile estimate) is essentially a hand-tuned controller; while Fig. 6 shows it works, there is no theoretical analysis or comparison to simpler alternatives (e.g., directly using the top-k quantile threshold, which the EMA term already computes).
